text: Not every administrative task actually requires full system access. A manager resetting passwords and updating a handful of fields for their team doesn't need the ability to rewrite business rules. A catalog owner adding new items doesn't need to touch ACLs or scheduled jobs. If full admin were the only administrative option available, every one of these ordinary requests would force a bad choice.

Delegated administration is ServiceNow's answer: a set of narrower, purpose-built administrative roles that let a non-full-admin user manage one specific slice of the platform. User_admin manages user records and group membership. Catalog_admin manages the Service Catalog — items, categories, variable sets. Report_admin manages reports and dashboards platform-wide. Real power in one area, and nothing outside it.

Each of these is a genuinely scoped grant, not just a smaller-sounding label. A user holding only catalog_admin cannot reset another user's password. A user holding only user_admin cannot touch a single catalog item. That hard boundary between domains is the entire point of delegated administration, and it's what makes it safe to hand out broadly.

This is least privilege applied at an organizational level, not just per record. Instead of asking whether someone needs to do administrative work at all, a careful administrator asks which specific function they need, and whether a narrower role already covers exactly that. And the containment habit from Lesson 3 still applies — check Contains Roles even on a scoped role, since a customized instance can configure one to grant more than its name implies.

When a request for more access comes in, work it like this: first identify the specific task the person actually needs to do. Second, check whether user_admin, catalog_admin, report_admin, or some other scoped role already covers it. Third, reserve full admin for requests that genuinely span multiple administrative domains at once, or for the rare case where no scoped role exists.

Defaulting to admin because it feels like the familiar, safe choice is actually the opposite — it's the choice that creates the most exposure if that account is ever compromised. Scoped roles let you say yes to routine administrative requests without over-granting. Next up: the Users, Groups & Roles lab, pulling all four lessons into one worked scenario.
